newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia defence chief vows to create efficient army.
newsitem.headline: Russia defence chief vows to create efficient army.

text.p: Russia's Defence Minister Igor Sergeyev vowed on Saturday to push through long-delayed military reforms to create leaner but more efficient armed forces and to ensure young soldiers did not forget the lessons of the past.

"I want Russia to have battle-ready armed forces and will apply every effort to achieve this goal," Sergeyev told reporters after attending an officers' graduation ceremony at a Moscow military academy.

"The army and navy can be reduced in size but still be battle-ready and capable of fulfilling their task of defending the state," he said. "Or they can be bigger but inefficient and incapable of fulfilling their tasks. I choose the first."
Sergeyev, whose predecessor Igor Rodionov was sacked last month for failing to push reforms, said the younger generation of officers had a crucial role to play in the reform process.
"It is important that these young lieutenants who were born after the war not only remember (the war) but have an active memory," he said. "We need to remember so we can draw conclusions and act."
Russia on Sunday marks the anniversary of Nazi Germany's assault on the Soviet Union in 1941. Russians still consider it one of the most solemn days of the year.
Earlier this week, Sergeyev declared war on waste in the army by committing himself to a long campaign to trim and modernise the cash-strapped, demoralised armed forces.

President Boris Yeltsin has said he wants the armed forces to be cut to 1.2 million from about 1.8 million men now. Even generals concede they are not sure of the exact figure, making it hard to assess progress on previous plans to cut 200,000 men this year.

On Saturday, General Anatoly Kvashnin, chief of the general staff and Sergeyev's number two in the defence establishment, told Interfax news agency that Russia should aim to reach 1.2 million by January 1999.

"In peace time the army has to correspond to the financial and economic capabilities of the country," he said. Echoing Sergeyev, Kvashnin said the main problem at present was the armed forces' lack of battle-readiness.
On Friday, Interfax quoted Deputy Prime Minister and Economy Minister Yakov Urinson as saying the government would boost defence spending next year to fund military reforms.

He said 94 trillion roubles ($16.3 billion) would be spent on the armed forces in 1998, up from 83 trillion in this year and 64 trillion in 1996. The new money would be targeted on new, modern equipment, research and combat training, Urinson said. ($1=5,761)
